Why is String final? How is immutability actually enforced?

final stops subclasses from overriding methods to break the guarantee, so any String parameter can be trusted. Enforcement: the value array is private and final, no method writes to it after construction, and every path in or out copies it. Being final alone would not be enough: the array contents would still be writable if a reference leaked. final on the field only fixes the reference.
Where is the string pool stored? Can its strings be garbage collected?

The String objects have been on the ordinary heap since Java 7; before that they were in PermGen, which caused OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space with heavy interning. The lookup structure, StringTable, is a native hash table with weak references, so a pooled String with no other references can be collected. Literals stay alive as long as the class that references them, through its resolved constants. The pool is not in Metaspace.
How many objects does String s = new String("hello"); create?

Up to two String objects: the pooled literal "hello", if it is not already pooled, and the new heap String. The new object shares the literal's byte[], so there is one backing array. If the literal is already in the pool, only one is created. new String("...") is almost never needed. It exists mainly for copying, and it was once useful for detaching a substring.
Output? String a = "hello"; String n = "hel"; final String f = "hel"; print(n + "lo" == a); print(f + "lo" == a); print((n + "lo").intern() == a);

true
n + "lo" is evaluated at runtime and gives a new object. f is a constant variable, so the expression folds to the literal "hello" at compile time. intern() returns the pooled instance. If f were assigned from a method call, it would be final but not constant, and the second line would be false. Verified.

Why does the "java".equals(s) style matter, and when would == on strings appear to work?

Calling equals on a constant avoids an NPE when s is null. == works only when both refer to the same object: literals, constants, or interned values. So tests with hard-coded values pass, while the code fails on data from HTTP, a database or substring, which are new objects. Static analysis such as SonarLint flags it.
What is the output? String a = "Java"; a.concat(" 21"); System.out.println(a);

Java. concat returns a new string that is thrown away. Same for toUpperCase, replace and trim. It is one of the most common bugs for newcomers. a = a.concat(" 21"); fixes it, and IDEs warn about ignored return values.
Output? System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5); System.out.println('a' + 'b' + "c"); System.out.println("Java".charAt(0) + "Java".charAt(1));

3345
195c

+ goes left to right. Numeric addition happens until a String is involved. The third has no String at all: charAt returns char, so 74 + 97 is the int 171.
What happens with String s = null; s += "x";, and with s.concat("x")?

+= gives "nullx", since concatenation converts null to the text "null". s.concat("x") throws NPE as it is a method call on null. Also "a".concat(null) throws NPE. null + null with literals does not compile, but with two null String variables gives "nullnull".
What did Java 9 change about concatenation? Should you still use StringBuilder?

javac emits invokedynamic to StringConcatFactory rather than a hard-coded builder chain. The JVM generates a strategy on first use, computes the exact length, and avoids the builder's resizing, so a simple a + b + c is at least as fast, and clearer. Use StringBuilder when accumulating across loop iterations or several statements. The compiler optimizes each expression separately, so a loop still gives O(n²).
Why does repeated += in a loop cost O(n²)?

Each iteration allocates a new string and copies the accumulated text. Copy costs add up as 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is about n²/2 characters. That also generates heavy garbage. A StringBuilder appends in amortized O(1) by keeping spare capacity and doubling, so the total is O(n).
What are compact strings? Does charAt become slower?

Since Java 9, Strings store a byte[] and a coder. Latin-1-only text uses one byte per char, otherwise two bytes per char. That cuts memory substantially for typical data, without API changes. charAt has one extra branch on the coder, which the JIT handles well, and in exchange memory is lower, so there is less GC work and better cache use. One non-Latin-1 character makes the entire string two-byte, so the savings depend on your data.
How did substring change over time, and why?

Up to Java 7u5 it shared the parent's char[] with an offset and count: O(1), but a tiny substring of a huge string kept the entire array alive, a well-known memory leak. People worked around it with new String(sub). From 7u6 it copies: O(k), and no leak, and the fields were removed from String.
What is the difference between trim() and strip()? isEmpty() and isBlank()?

trim removes characters up to U+0020, which predates Unicode awareness, so it keeps U+2003 (em space) while removing control characters. strip (Java 11) uses Character.isWhitespace, so " x ".trim().length() is 3 and strip gives 1. isEmpty tests length 0; isBlank also accepts only-whitespace strings.
replace vs replaceAll: which replaces all occurrences?

Both do. The name misleads: replace treats both arguments literally, and replaceAll treats the first as a regex and the second as a replacement template. "a.b.c".replaceAll(".", "-") gives -----. Use replace unless you need a regex. It also avoids compiling a pattern.
What does "a,b,,c,,".split(",").length give? And "".split(",").length?

4 and 1. Trailing empty strings are removed when the limit is 0 (the default), while interior ones remain. An input with no match returns the whole input as one element, so the empty string gives one empty string, even though that looks odd. To keep all columns of a CSV line, use split(",", -1). For real CSV with quoted fields, use a library.
How does compareTo work? Can it return something other than -1, 0, 1?

It returns the difference of the first unequal chars, or of the lengths if one is a prefix of the other. "a".compareTo("A") is 32, and "apple".compareTo("apple pie") is -4. Only the sign is contractually meaningful. So test < 0, never == -1. It orders by UTF-16 code unit, so "Z" sorts before "a". Use Collator for human sorting.
Why can toLowerCase() break a program on some servers?

It uses the default locale. With a Turkish default, "TITLE" becomes "tıtle", with a dotless ı, so "TITLE".toLowerCase().equals("title") is false, and enum lookups or header comparisons fail. Use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for identifiers and protocols, and equalsIgnoreCase for comparison. Length may change as well: "ß" uppercases to "SS".
StringBuilder default capacity? How does it grow? What does new StringBuilder('a') do?

Default capacity is 16, or the length + 16 for a String argument. It grows to about (old × 2) + 2: 16, 34, 70 in the run above. new StringBuilder('a') compiles because char widens to int, picking the capacity constructor: the result is empty with capacity 97. This is a known trap: new StringBuilder('H').append("ello") gives "ello", because the H is lost.
Is StringBuffer ever the right choice?

Rarely. Each method is synchronized, but a sequence of calls is not atomic, so check-then-append remains unsafe, and the order of interleaved appends from threads is usually useless. In practice each thread builds its own text, then shares the immutable result. It remains in legacy APIs. If you ever need a truly shared buffer, use an explicit lock or a queue of strings.
Why does sb1.equals(sb2) return false for equal content? How do you compare?

StringBuilder inherits identity-based equals from Object. Mutable objects make unsafe keys, and a content-based hash would change. Compare using sb1.compareTo(sb2) == 0 (Java 11), sb1.toString().contentEquals(sb2), or "text".contentEquals(sb).
What is the difference between String.join, StringJoiner and Collectors.joining?

String.join covers a delimiter over an array or Iterable. StringJoiner adds a prefix, suffix, an empty value, incremental add, and merge. Collectors.joining is the stream collector built on the same idea. Note that String.join prints nulls as "null", and none of them skips nulls for you.
How does a text block decide its indentation? Output of this one?

String s = """
        a
      b""";
It equals "  a\nb". The compiler takes the minimum indentation of non-blank lines, and the closing delimiter's line if it stands alone. Here b has 6 spaces, the minimum, so 6 are removed from both lines. No final newline, because the delimiter is on the same line as b. Trailing spaces are stripped unless written \s, and a backslash at line end joins lines. A text block is an ordinary compile-time String constant, so it is pooled.
String.format vs concatenation vs StringBuilder: when to use each?

Concatenation for simple one-liners. StringBuilder for loops. format or formatted for alignment, padding, number or date formatting, or templates. format is far slower since it parses the format string at runtime, so avoid it on hot paths. For logging, use parameterized messages such as log.debug("id={}", id), which skip formatting if the level is off.
Why might String.format("%.2f", 1.5) produce "1,50"?

Without a locale argument it uses the default FORMAT locale, and many locales use a decimal comma. That breaks CSV exports, generated SQL and JSON built by hand. Pass Locale.ROOT for machine-readable output. Parsing has the same problem in the other direction.
What does "%.2f" give for 0.125 and 0.135? And DecimalFormat("#.#") for 0.25?

0.13, 0.14, and 0.2. Formatter rounds HALF_UP on the exact decimal value of the double. 0.125 is exactly representable, so its tie rounds up. DecimalFormat defaults to HALF_EVEN, so the tie 0.25 goes to the even 0.2. Non-representable values are not ties at all. If rounding rules matter, use BigDecimal with an explicit mode, or call setRoundingMode.
matches() vs find() vs lookingAt()? Why does "hello".matches("ell") return false?

matches needs the entire input to match, acting as if anchored at both ends. find searches for the next occurrence. lookingAt anchors only at the start. "hello".matches("ell") is false, while "hello".matches(".*ell.*") or contains("ell") works. "a\nb".matches("a.b") is also false, unless DOTALL is set.
Is Pattern thread-safe? Is Matcher?

Pattern is immutable, so share it as a static final constant. Matcher holds position and group state, and is not thread-safe, so create one per use with pattern.matcher(input). matcher.reset(newInput) can reuse one in a single thread.
Greedy vs lazy vs possessive quantifiers?

Greedy (.*) takes the maximum and backs off on failure. Lazy (.*?) takes the minimum and expands on failure. Possessive (.*+) takes the maximum and never backs off, so it fails faster but can miss matches: "aaa".matches("a*+a") is false. On <a><b>, <.+> matches the whole text, and <.+?> matches only <a>. A negated class such as <[^>]+> is often better than either.
What is ReDoS? Is (a+)+b dangerous in Java?

ReDoS is a denial of service through an input that makes a backtracking regex take exponential time, tying up a request thread. (a+)+b is the classic example, and it is exponential in many engines, including Java 8. Since JDK 9 the engine memoizes in group loops, and it finished in under 1 ms on Java 21 even for 28 a's. Adding a backreference, (a+)+\1b, restores exponential behaviour: 8 seconds at 28 a's in our run. So the danger is narrower but real. Mitigate with input length limits, no user-supplied patterns, possessive quantifiers, a deadline-checking CharSequence, or RE2/J.

"😀".length() is 2. Why? How do you count characters correctly?

length() counts UTF-16 code units, and U+1F600 is above U+FFFF, so it needs a surrogate pair. codePointCount(0, s.length()) gives 1. Code points are not user-visible characters either: "é" is 2 code points shown as one letter, and some emoji sequences are many code points joined. To count what a user perceives, use the \X regex (2 matches for an accented letter plus an emoji) or BreakIterator.
How many bytes is "café" in UTF-8? What does getBytes() with no argument do?

5: é takes 2 bytes. In ISO-8859-1 it takes 4, and in UTF_16 10, including the byte order mark. getBytes() uses the default charset: UTF-8 since Java 18, and the platform's setting before. On older JDKs, this is a classic cause of "works on Linux, breaks on Windows". Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8.
Users' names show as "Ã©" on the page. How do you debug it?

"Ã©" is the signature of UTF-8 bytes decoded as Latin-1 or Windows-1252. Follow the data: log the hex of the bytes at each hop. Check the browser's request encoding and Content-Type, servlet filter or Spring's CharacterEncodingFilter, the JDBC connection settings, the column charset (utf8mb4), and the response header. Fix the wrong decode where it occurs. If bad data is already stored, it may be repairable with a re-encode as long as no bytes were replaced, but test it, because a double conversion corrupts good rows.
Why is a char[] preferred to a String for passwords? Is it really safer?

A String cannot be cleared, and it stays in memory until GC, possibly longer if pooled, so a heap dump exposes it. A char[] can be zeroed after use, and does not print its content by accident. But it only reduces exposure: GC can leave copies, and frameworks handle passwords as Strings before your code runs. In web apps, focus on TLS, hashing with BCrypt or Argon2, not logging, and protecting dumps.
Is String a good HashMap key? Why? What about StringBuilder or char[]?

Excellent: immutable, so the hash never changes, and it is cached after the first call, so repeated lookups only compute it once. equals is well defined. StringBuilder and char[] use identity hashing, so an equal-content lookup misses, and they are mutable. Convert to String first.
What does switch on a String do for hash collisions such as "Aa" and "BB"?
The compiler generates a lookupswitch on hashCode(), and each hash bucket holds equals checks for all labels with that hash. Both labels work correctly: a collision only adds one extra comparison.
Can you change a String's content through reflection? Would it be safe?

On modern JDKs, not without --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED, since JDK internals are strongly encapsulated (InaccessibleObjectException). Even if opened, it corrupts the program: pooled literals are shared across all classes, the cached hash becomes stale, and the JIT trusts final fields of String. So the answer is "technically possible with explicit opening, and never appropriate".
What is the maximum length of a String? Of a literal?

The API uses int lengths, so the theoretical maximum is about 231-1 chars; UTF-16 content is limited to about half, because the backing byte[] holds two bytes per char. Available heap and the VM's array limit apply. A literal is limited by the class-file format to 65,535 bytes of modified UTF-8, giving a "constant string too long" compile error. Load large text from a resource file.
Scenario: an app holds many duplicate strings and heap usage is high. What are your options?

- Take a heap dump, and check duplicates in Eclipse MAT.
- Ask whether the data needs to be strings at all: enums, or IDs as long.
- Enable -XX:+UseStringDeduplication with G1. It is a one-line change that shares byte[] arrays in the background. It has a small CPU cost.
- Canonicalize in code when parsing: a HashMap or bounded cache, or intern for a small, stable value set.
- Do not keep substrings of large documents, or keep parsed fields rather than raw JSON.
Scenario: a service spends a lot of CPU in string handling for log lines. What do you look at?

Profile first, for example with Java Flight Recorder or async-profiler. Common causes: building messages when the level is disabled (use {} placeholders rather than +), String.format on hot paths, replaceAll or split with a regex compiled on each call (use a static final Pattern), += in loops, default-size builders that keep resizing, and serializing whole objects into logs. Fix what the profile shows rather than guessing.

What is the time complexity of indexOf, contains, substring, equals and hashCode?

substring is O(k), since it copies. equals is O(n) in the worst case, but returns immediately on identity or a length difference. hashCode is O(n) once, then O(1) from the cache. length and charAt are O(1). indexOf(String) and contains use a simple scan with a JVM intrinsic: O(n × m) worst case, but very fast in practice.
Why is string concatenation in SQL dangerous even if you escape quotes yourself?

Hand-written escaping is fragile. It misses encodings, backslash rules that differ between databases, numeric contexts where there are no quotes (WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1), and second-order injection, where stored data is concatenated later. A bind parameter (? in PreparedStatement, :name in JPQL, or a Spring Data method) sends the value separately from the SQL text, so it can never be parsed as SQL. The database can also cache the plan. Identifiers such as column names in ORDER BY cannot be bound, so check them against a whitelist. Watch for concatenation inside @Query(nativeQuery = true) and createNativeQuery as well.
Is URLEncoder.encode the right way to build a URL?

Only for query parameter values, and even then it applies application/x-www-form-urlencoded rules: a space becomes +, not %20. That is wrong inside a path segment, and some servers do not decode + as a space. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8; the overload with no charset is deprecated. To build a whole URI, use UriComponentsBuilder or UriBuilder in Spring, which encode each component by its own rules. Never encode an entire URL string at once, because that also encodes :, / and ?.

Why compare API keys or HMAC signatures with MessageDigest.isEqual instead of equals?

String.equals and Arrays.equals stop at the first mismatch, so a response is slightly faster when more leading characters are wrong. With many measurements, an attacker can use that timing side channel to recover a secret one byte at a time. MessageDigest.isEqual(byte[], byte[]) compares in time that does not depend on where the bytes differ. Even better, store a hash of API keys rather than the raw keys, and compare the hashes.

| String.valueOf(obj) | obj.toString() | "" + obj | Objects.toString(obj, "-")
obj is null | "null" | NullPointerException | "null" | "-"
Primitives | Overloads, no boxing | Needs a wrapper | Works | Boxes
Reads as | Explicit conversion | Explicit call | A trick | Explicit, with a default
Object o = null;
String.valueOf(o);      // "null"
String.valueOf(null);   // NPE: picks valueOf(char[]) as the most specific overload
Rule of thumb: use String.valueOf or Objects.toString(o, default) when the value may be null. Watch out: a literal "null" in a log or a database column usually means one of these ran on a null.
split vs StringTokenizer vs Scanner vs Pattern.splitAsStream?

| String.split | StringTokenizer | Scanner | Pattern.splitAsStream
Delimiter | Regex | A set of single characters | Regex (whitespace by default) | Regex
Empty tokens | Kept, except trailing ones | Skipped | Skipped for whitespace | Kept, except trailing ones
Result | String[] | Iteration with nextToken() | Typed reads: nextInt(), ... | Lazy Stream<String>
Status | Normal | Legacy | For input parsing, slower | Normal
Rule of thumb: use split for everyday work, and escape regex characters (split("\\.") or Pattern.quote). In a hot loop, compile the Pattern once and reuse it. Use Scanner for reading typed input, not for splitting strings.
equals vs equalsIgnoreCase vs contentEquals vs regionMatches?

| equals | equalsIgnoreCase | contentEquals | regionMatches
Other side | Any Object; true only for a String | String | Any CharSequence (e.g. StringBuilder) | Part of a String
Case | Sensitive | Ignored, char by char | Sensitive | Your choice (boolean flag)
Locale | Not used | Not used | Not used | Not used
Example | "a".equals(sb) is false | "ß" vs "SS" is false | "a".contentEquals(sb) is true | Compare a prefix without substring
Rule of thumb: prefer equalsIgnoreCase over toLowerCase().equals(); it allocates nothing and avoids the locale trap. For language-aware comparison (sorting names, accents), use java.text.Collator.

Unit | UTF-16 char | UTF-16 unit as int | Unicode code point as int
Emoji such as 😀 | Two chars (a surrogate pair) | Two values | One value
Memory | Copies the whole string | No copy, lazy IntStream | No copy, lazy IntStream
Good for | In-place algorithms (reverse, sort) | ASCII-only counting | Correct handling of any text
"a😀".chars().count();        // 3
"a😀".codePoints().count();   // 2
String s = new StringBuilder().appendCodePoint(0x1F600).toString();
Interview tip: neither counts what a user sees as one character: an emoji with a skin-tone modifier is several code points. For that, use a BreakIterator or the regex \X.
